17       Presently before the Court is Plaintiff Upper Deck Company’s (“Upper Deck”) 
18  renewed motion to seal.  (ECF No. 114.)  For the reasons below, the Court GRANTS IN 
19  PART and DENIES IN PART Upper Deck’s motion in accordance with Appendix A.   
20  I.   BACKGROUND                                                           
21       Defendant Pixels.com (“Pixels”) allegedly interfered with Upper Deck’s exclusive 
22  rights  to  use  intellectual  property  assets  associated  with  the  brand  of  world-famous 
23  basketball  player,  Michael  Jordan  (“Jordan”),  to  develop  sports  memorabilia.    More 
24  specifically, Pixels allegedly advertised and sold products appropriating Jordan’s likeness 
25  online without either Upper Deck’s or Jordan’s permission.  (ECF No. 24 ¶¶ 25–35.)  Upper 
26  Deck obtained the rights to use Michael Jordan’s likeness through licensing agreements.  
27  (Id. ¶¶19–24.)  Furthermore, Pixels’ products also allegedly misappropriated Upper Deck’s 
28  own trademarks—including Upper Deck’s logo.  (Id. ¶ 11.)                  
1       On May 28, 2024, Upper Deck initiated this action against Defendant Pixels.com 
2  (“Pixels”).  (ECF No. 1.)  On October 1, 2024, Upper Deck filed the operative complaint 
3  in this action alleging causes of action, inter alia, for: (1) false advertising and unfair 
4  competition claims under the Lanham Act, 15 U.S.C.A. § 1125(a); (2) trademark dilution 
5  under the Lanham Act, 15 U.S.C.A. § 1125(c); (3) trademark infringement under 15 
6  U.S.C.A.  §  1114;  (4)  deprivation  of  rights  of  publicity,  Cal.  Civ.  Code  §  3344;  (5) 
7  deprivation of rights of publicity under California common law; (6) unfair competition 
8  under California statutory, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200 et seq, and common law.  (ECF 
9  No. 24.)                                                                  
10       Throughout the course of this action, both parties filed motions to seal.  (See ECF 
11  Nos. 75, 78, 81, 88, 91, 95, 97, 102, 107.)  The Court partially ruled on Parties’ proposed 
12  redactions and ordered for Parties to file a consolidated motion to seal on July 28, 2025.  
13  (ECF No. 110.)  Upper Deck filed a motion to seal, consolidating prior motions, on August 
14  8, 2025.  (ECF No. 114.)  Upper Deck moved to seal specific portions of certain documents, 
15  including:                                                                
16    1.  An executed licensing agreement between Upper Deck and Jump 23 regarding 
17       Upper Deck’s rights to use Michael Jordan’s intellectual property in its products 
18       (ECF Nos. 75 and 78, Ex. 7);                                         
19    2.  An executed agreement between Upper Deck and Brevettar, LLC for Brevettar, LLC 
20       to sublicense Upper Deck’s rights to use Michael Jordan’s intellectual property (ECF 
21       Nos. 75, 78, Ex. 10);                                                
22    3.  An executed agreement between Brevettar, LLC and Trends International, LLC for 
23       Trends International, LLC to sublicense Brevettar, LLC’s rights to use Michael 
24       Jordan’s intellectual property (ECF No. 78, Ex. 20);                 
25    4.  An expert report by Upper Deck’s expert, Christian Tregillis (ECF No. 78, Ex. 94); 
26    5.  An expert rebuttal report by Christian Tregillis (ECF No. 78, Ex. 98);  
27    6.  An email between Jump 23 and Upper Deck management attached to Pixels’ motion 
28       to seal (ECF No. 75, Ex. 105); and                                   
1    7.  An expert report by Pixels’ expert, Lindsey Fisher (ECF No. 102, Ex. M).  
2       Upper Deck also moved to seal certain documents in their entirety—including a 
3  report of Pixels’ sales data (ECF No. 102, Ex. F).  Pixels filed a response on August 13, 
4  2025.  (ECF No. 123.)  In this Order, the Court evaluates Upper Deck’s motion to seal.  
5  (ECF No. 114.)                                                            
6  II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                       
7       “[T]he courts of this country recognize a general right to inspect and copy public 
8  records and documents, including judicial records and documents.”  Nixon v. Warner 
9  Commc’ns, Inc., 435 U.S. 589, 597 (1978).  “Unless a particular court record is one 
10  ‘traditionally kept secret,’ a ‘strong presumption in favor of access’ is the starting point.” 
11  Kamakana v. City & Cnty. of Honolulu, 447 F.3d 1172, 1178 (9th Cir. 2006) (citing Foltz 
12  v. State Farm Mut. Auto Ins. Co., 331 F.3d 1122, 1135 (9th Cir. 2003)).  “The presumption 
13  of  access  is  ‘based  on  the  need  for  federal  courts,  although  independent—indeed, 
14  particularly because they are independent—to have a measure of accountability and for the 
15  public to have confidence in the administration of justice.’”  Ctr. for Auto Safety v. Chrysler 
16  Grp., LLC, 809 F.3d 1092, 1096 (9th Cir. 2016) (quoting United States v. Amodeo, 71 F.3d 
17  1044, 1048 (2d Cir. 1995)).                                               
18       A party seeking to seal a judicial record bears the burden of overcoming the strong 
19  presumption of access.  Foltz, 331 F.3d at 1135. The showing required to meet this burden 
20  depends upon whether the documents to be sealed relate to a motion that is “more than 
21  tangentially related to the merits of the case.”  Ctr. for Auto Safety, 809 F.3d at 1101.  When 
22  the underlying motion is more than tangentially related to the merits, the “compelling 
23  reasons” standard applies. Id. at 1096–98.  When the underlying motion does not surpass 
24  the tangential relevance threshold, the “good cause” standard applies.  Id. 
25       “In general, ‘compelling reasons’ sufficient to outweigh the public’s interest in 
26  disclosure and justify sealing court records exist when such ‘court files might have become 
27  a vehicle for improper purposes,’ such as the use of records to gratify private spite, promote 
28  public scandal, circulate libelous statements, or release trade secrets.”  Kamakana, 447 
1  F.3d at 1179 (quoting Nixon, 435 U.S. at 598).  As to this last category, courts have been 
2  willing to seal court filings containing confidential business material, “such as marketing 
3  strategies, product development plans, licensing agreements, and profit, cost, and margin 
4  data,” where the parties have been able to point to concrete factual information to justify 
5  sealing.  See, e.g., Cohen v. Trump, No. 13-cv-2519-GPC-WVG, 2016 WL 3036302, at *5 
6  (S.D. Cal. May 27, 2016).  However, “[t]he mere fact that the production of records may 
7  lead to a litigant’s embarrassment, incrimination, or exposure to further litigation will not, 
8  without  more,  compel  the  court  to  seal  its  records.”    Kamakana,  447  F.3d  at  1179. 
9  Similarly, it is not enough to “mention[] a general category of privilege, without any further 
10  elaboration or any specific linkage with the documents.”  Id. at 1184.  A blanket protective 
11  order is not itself sufficient to show “good cause,” let alone compelling reasons, for sealing 
12  particular documents.  See Foltz, 331 F.3d at 1133; San Jose Mercury News, Inc. v. U.S. 
13  Dist. Ct., N. Dist., 187 F.3d 1096, 1103 (9th Cir. 1999).  The decision to seal documents is 
14  “one best left to the sound discretion of the trial court” upon consideration of the “relevant 
15  facts and circumstances of the particular case.”  Nixon, 435 U.S. at 599. 
16       In addition, parties moving to seal documents must comply with the procedures set 
17  forth in this Court’s Standing Order for filing documents under seal.  See Standing Order 
18  of the Hon. Cynthia Bashant for Civil Cases § 5.  These procedures limit sealing to “only 
19  those documents, or portions thereof, necessary to protect such sensitive information.”  Id. 
20  Thus,  although  sometimes  it  may  be  appropriate  to  seal  a  document  in  its  entirety, 
21  whenever possible, a party must redact.  See Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1183 (noting a 
22  preference for redactions so long as they “have the virtue of being limited and clear”); 
23  Murphy v. Kavo Am. Corp., No. 11-cv-00410-YGR, 2012 WL 1497489, at *2–3 (N.D. Cal. 
24  Apr. 27, 2012) (denying motion to seal exhibits but directing parties to redact confidential 
25  information).                                                             
26  III.  ANALYSIS                                                            
27       A.   Whether Upper Deck Corrected Procedural Deficiencies Identified in 
28            ECF No. 110                                                     
1            1.   Requirement  for  Parties  to  Confer  and  Submit  Responses  to 
2            Support Relevant Motions to Seal                                
3       The Court’s Standing Order notes, “[t]he fact that both sides agree to seal a document 
4  or that a stipulated protective order was issued is insufficient cause for sealing.” Standing 
5  Order § 5.A (“§ 5.A”).  “Parties often seek to seal a document only because another party 
6  designated the document as sensitive under a protective order . . . [i]n these circumstances, 
7  the moving party must first meet and confer with the designating party to determine 
8  whether the designating party maintains that any portion of the document must be filed 
9  under seal.”  Id.  Then, “the designating party must file a response to the sealing motion 
10  within seven days that satisfies the sealing standard . . . If no response is filed, the Court 
11  may order that the document be filed in the public record.”  Id.          
12       Because Upper Deck is the moving party for the present motion to seal (ECF No. 
13  114), the designating party’s burden to respond to a sealing motion in § 5.A only applies 
14  to documents in which Pixels is the designating party.  In Upper Deck’s renewed motion 
15  to seal and accompanying papers, Upper Decks’ attorney has indicated that the above 
16  documents were designated as “‘CONFIDENTIAL’ and/or ‘CONFIDENTIAL – FOR   
17  COUNSEL ONLY’ materials under the Protective Order by Upper Deck and/or Pixels.”  
18  (ECF No. 114-1 ¶ 2 (emphasis added).)  From this, it is not clear which party had made the 
19  confidentiality designations.  Regardless, Pixels has filed an appropriate response (ECF 
20  No. 123) to all of the documents that Upper Deck has moved to seal in its renewed motion 
21  (ECF No. 114).  Accordingly, the Court now finds that § 5.A of the Standing Order does 
22  not necessitate the dismissal of any of Upper Deck’s motion to seal.      
23            2.   Requirement to Publicly File Copies of Documents with Proposed 
24            Redactions                                                      
25       Since  the  Court’s  last  order  on  Parties’  motions  to  seal  (ECF  No.  110),  the 
26  documents Upper Deck seeks to redact are correctly lodged on the public docket.  (See 
27  ECF Nos. 110 at 4:26–5:7 (citing ECF Nos. 75, 78, 88, 97, and 107); 76 (lodged ECF No. 
28  75), 82 (lodged ECF No. 78); 89 (lodged ECF No. 88); 98 (lodged ECF No. 97); 108 
1  (lodged ECF No. 107); ECF Nos. 103-3 (lodged ECF No. 102, Ex. F); 103-5 (lodged ECF 
2  No. 102, Ex. M).)  Accordingly, since Upper Deck seeks to seal those same documents in 
3  its renewed motion to seal (ECF No. 114), the Court now turns to evaluate whether Upper 
4  Deck’s  justifications  for  sealing  or  redacting  those  documents  provide  sufficiently 
5  compelling reasons for sealing pursuant to caselaw.                       
6       B.   Whether  Upper  Deck  Presents  Compelling  Reasons  for  its  Proposed 
7            Redactions                                                      
8            1.   Related Documents More Than Tangentially Related to Merits  
9       As the Court previously found (ECF No. 110 at 4:6-16), Upper Deck’s proposed 
10  documents to seal are filed in connection with Parties’ summary judgment motions (ECF 
11  Nos. 74, 79).  See Pac. Marine Propellers, Inc. v. Wartsila Def., Inc., No. 17-CV-555-L-
12  NLS, 2018 WL 11457880, at *1 (S.D. Cal. Nov. 5, 2018) (“The compelling reasons 
13  standard applies to all motions except those that are only ‘tangentially related to the merits 
14  of a case.’. . .  Defendants’ summary judgment motion is more than tangentially related to 
15  the merits”) (citing Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1179).  As such, the Court finds Upper Deck’s 
16  renewed motion to seal (ECF No. 114) is subject to the “compelling reasons” standard in 
17  Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1179.                                               
18            2.   “Compelling Reasons” Legal Standard                        
19       Preventing the release of trade secrets generally constitutes a compelling reason to 
20  seal such documents.  Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1179; see also Nixon, 435 U.S. at 598 
21  (observing that the “common-law right of inspection has bowed before the power of a court 
22  to insure that its records” are not used as “sources of business information that might harm 
23  a litigant's competitive standing”);  Apple Inc. v. Samsung Elecs. Co., 727 F.3d 1214, 1226–
24  28  (Fed.Cir.2013)  (holding  that  under  Ninth  Circuit  law,  detailed  product-specific 
25  information and internal reports are appropriate to seal under the “compelling reasons” 
26  standard where that information could be used to the company's competitive disadvantage). 
27       A  “trade  secret  may  consist  of  any  formula,  pattern,  device  or  compilation  of 
28  information  which  is  used  in  [the  party]'s  business,  and  which  gives  [the  party]  an 
1  opportunity to obtain an advantage over competitors who do not know or use it.”  In re 
2  Elec. Arts, Inc., 298 F. App'x 568, 569–70 (9th Cir. 2008) (citing Restatement of Torts § 
3  757, cmt. B); see also Clark v. Bunker, 453 F.2d 1006, 1009 (9th Cir.1972) (adopting the 
4  Restatement  definition  and  finding  that  “a  detailed  plan  for  the  creation,  promotion, 
5  financing, and sale of contracts” constitutes a trade secret); Whyte v. Schlage Lock Co., 101 
6  Cal.App.4th 1443, 1455-56, 125 Cal.Rptr.2d 277 (2002).                    
7       Even if proposed material for sealing does not constitute a trade secret, it may still 
8  be sealable as confidential business information.  See In re Elec. Arts, Inc., 298 F. App'x at 
9  569  (finding  sealable  “business  information  that  might  harm  a  litigant's  competitive 
10  standing”); see also Ctr. for Auto Safety, 809 F.3d at 1097 (citing Nixon, 435 U.S. at 598–
11  599) (“sources of business information that might harm a litigant's competitive standing” 
12  are subject to sealing); see also In re Qualcomm Litig., No. 3:17-cv-0108-GPC-MDD, 2017 
13  WL 5176922, at *2 (S.D. Cal. Nov. 8, 2017) (sealing is warranted to prevent competitors 
14  from “gaining insight into the parties' business model and strategy”); see also Garrity 
15  Power Servs. LLC v. Samsung Elecs. Co., No. 21-MC-80159-JSC, 2021 WL 3473937, at 
16  *1 (N.D. Cal. July 29, 2021) (“confidential business information in the form of ‘license 
17  agreements, financial terms, details of confidential licensing negotiations, and business 
18  strategies’ is sealable”).                                                
19       However, not all business information is so confidential or sensitive that it must be 
20  sealed.  See, e.g., Open Text S.A. v. Box, Inc., No. 13-04910, 2014 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 
21  177484, 2014 WL 7368594, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 26, 2014) (declining to seal, for example, 
22  information about a litigant's "product design and source code and highly confidential and 
23  competitively sensitive business information including usage data," in the absence of 
24  demonstrating “specific compelling reasons”); GoDaddy.com LLC v. RPost Commc'ns 
25  Ltd., No. 14-00126, 2014 WL 2117349, at *1 (D. Ariz. May 21, 2014) ("[A] party's 
26  allegations that material is 'confidential' or 'business information' are insufficient to justify 
27  sealing court records containing such material unless the party proves the existence of 
28                                                                            
1  compelling reasons such as those set forth in Kamakana.... "[O]nly in extremely limited 
2  circumstances will confidential information actually merit the sealing of court records.").  
3       In the Ninth Circuit, trade secrets, specific pricing terms, royalty rates, and similar 
4  data are commonly sealed.  See, e.g., In re Elec. Arts, Inc., 298 F. App'x 568, 569 (9th 
5  Cir. 2008).  For information that falls outside of those categories, movants must 
6  particularly allege how their proposed redactions relate to confidential information that 
7  should be sealed.  See Perez v. Blue Mountain Farms, No. 2:13-CV-5081-RMP, 2015 
8  WL 11112413, at *4 (E.D. Wash. Sept. 28, 2015) (“Defendants' redactions and any 
9  claims of privilege or withholding of information must be explained with particularity as 
10  to why that information should be protected pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5)(A)”); see 
11  also Ketayi v. Health Enrollment Grp., No. 3:20-CV-1198-RSH-KSC, 2023 WL  
12  12007132, at *2 (S.D. Cal. June 28, 2023)  (“Compelling reasons may exist to seal some 
13  of the redacted information in this record as confidential business information, but not for 
14  the broad redactions HII proposes.”).                                     
15       Importantly, “[t]he proponent of sealing bears the burden with respect to sealing. A 
16  failure to meet that burden means that the default posture of public access prevails.”  
17  Kamakana v. City & County of Honolulu, 447 F.3d 1172, 1182 (9th Cir. 2006). 
18            3.   “Narrowly Tailored” Legal Standard                         
19       “Only those documents, or portions thereof, necessary to protect such sensitive 
20  information” may be sealed. Standing Order § 5.A. As such, whenever possible, the 
21  moving party must redact only what is necessary.  See Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1183; 
22  Murphy, 2012 WL 1497489, at *2–3.  Redactions must be narrowly tailored such that only 
23  information that meets the compelling reasons standard is redacted. See Kamakana, 447 
24  F.3d at 1183 (highlighting the “limited and clear” nature and specificity of the redactions); 
25  ImprimisRx, LLC v. OSRX, Inc., No. 21-cv-01305-BAS-DL, 2023 WL 7029210, at *4 
26  (S.D. Cal. Oct. 24, 2023) (rejecting redactions that were insufficiently tailored). The 
27  moving party must provide the compelling reason justifying the proposed redactions. Foltz, 
28  331 F.3d at 1135.                                                         
1       Litigation predicated upon contracts cannot be conducted in secret. JBS Packerland, 
2  Inc. v. Phillips Cattle Co., Inc., No. 24-cv-01299-BAS-MSB, 2024 WL 4280960, at *2 
3  (S.D. Cal. Sept. 24, 2024).  The public has the right to know the gist of the underlying 
4  agreements in order to understand the court’s rulings.  Id.  Accordingly, mere vague or 
5  ambiguous references to sealed documents, without any discussion of the substance of the 
6  sealed documents, do not meet the compelling reasons standard.  See Nia v. Bank of Am., 
7  N.A., No. 21-cv-1799-BAS-BGS, 2024 WL 171659, at *9 (S.D. Cal. Jan. 12, 2024); 
8  ImprimisRx, LLC, 2023 WL 7029210, at *5.  Information already available to the public 
9  also cannot meet the compelling reasons standard.  See id. at 1184.       
10            4.   Analysis of Compelling Reasons                             
11                 i.   Financial Data (e.g., Gross Revenue Amount, and Sales Data) 
12                 and Damages Calculation                                    
13       “Sales data may constitute a trade secret if it is not readily ascertainable from a public 
14  source but instead developed with a substantial amount of time, effort, and money.”  Yeiser 
15  Rsch. & Dev. LLC v. Teknor Apex Co., 281 F. Supp. 3d 1021, 1046 (S.D. Cal. 2017).  Here, 
16  it is apparent that Pixels has expended substantial effort to calculate its sales data and gross 
17  revenue from the various spreadsheets, tables, and expert reports Upper Deck moves to 
18  seal.  The Court has also previously found that Pixels’ financial data is subject to sealing.  
19  (ECF No. 110 at 10:21–11:20.)                                             
20       Thus, the Court GRANTS Upper Deck’s request to seal Pixels’ financial data—
21  including in sealing Exhibit F to Upper Deck’s motion to seal (ECF No. 102), which the 
22  Court has previously found to be sealable (ECF No. 110 at 11:4-6).  Along the same vein, 
23  the  Court  also  GRANTS  sealing  experts’  damages  calculations  based  upon  Pixels’ 
24  financial data.  (Id. at 10:21–11:20.)                                    
25                 ii.  Licensing Agreement Terms                             
26       The Ninth Circuit has held that licensing agreement terms are sealable trade secrets 
27  when such terms provide a plan for the formation and sale of contracts.  In re Elec. Arts, 
28  Inc., 298 F. App'x at 569–70 (finding license agreement to be a trade secret); France 
1  Telecom S.A. v. Marvell Semiconductor Inc., No. 12-CV-04967-WHO, 2014 WL 4965995, 
2  at *3 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 3, 2014) (“the information at issue—terms of a license agreement—
3  constitutes trade secrets and is properly sealed”).  Those terms may constitute trade secrets 
4  because their public disclosure may hinder the trade secret holder’s market competitiveness 
5  and participation.  See e.g., In re NCAA Student-Athlete Name & Likeness Licensing Litig., 
6  No. C 09-1967 CW, 2014 WL 662545, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 20, 2014) (“Because the public 
7  disclosure of some of these terms may undermine NCAA's ability to negotiate future 
8  licensing agreements with other broadcasters, these terms may be sealed.”).  
9       However, there are limitations on the extent to which terms of a licensing agreement 
10  can be sealed.  For example, if certain terms are “otherwise publicly known,” they may not 
11  be sealable.  Huawei Techs., Co, Ltd v. Samsung Elecs. Co, Ltd., 340 F. Supp. 3d 934, 1004 
12  (N.D.  Cal.  2018).    Additionally,  if  terms  of  licensing  agreements  that  appear  to  be 
13  boilerplate contractual terms, courts may require the moving party to “explain[] why 
14  [those] provisions are so unique to that agreement that disclosure would cause significant 
15  harm.”  Id.  Further, even when courts have found licensing terms to constitute trade 
16  secrets, they have still limited permissible redactions to only specific portions of those 
17  clauses.  In re NCAA Student-Athlete Name & Likeness Licensing Litig., 2014 WL 662545, 
18  at *1 (“only the specific dollar amounts. . . may be sealed”); O'Bannon v. Nat'l Collegiate 
19  Athletic Ass'n, No. C 09-3329 CW, 2014 WL 12997312, at *1 (N.D. Cal. June 10, 2014) 
20  (same).                                                                   
21                      a.   Royalty   Rate,  Minimum     Guarantee,  and     
22                      Compensation Clauses                                  
23       It is well-established in the Ninth Circuit that “pricing terms, royalty rates, and 
24  guaranteed minimum payment terms” are sealable trade secrets.  In re Elec. Arts, Inc., 298 
25  F. App'x at 569–70; see also Clark v. Bunker, 453 F.2d 1006, 1009 (9th Cir.1972) (adopting 
26  the Restatement definition and finding that “a detailed plan for the creation, promotion, 
27  financing, and sale of contracts” constitutes a trade secret) (citing Whyte v. Schlage Lock 
28  Co., 101 Cal.App.4th 1443, 1455-56, 125 Cal.Rptr.2d 277 (2002)).          
1       Thus, the Court GRANTS sealing the specific numerical values of royalty rate 
2  minimum guarantee and compensation terms.  See In re NCAA Student-Athlete Name & 
3  Likeness Licensing Litig., 2014 WL 662545, at *1 (“only the specific dollar amounts. . . 
4  may be sealed”); O'Bannon, 2014 WL 12997312, at *1 (same).  To clarify, the numerical 
5  values of royalty rates, minimum guarantee, and compensation should also be sealed in 
6  other documents (such as expert reports) discussing those values.         
7                      b.   Sample Review and Approval                       
8       Upper Deck also moves to redact the number of sample products that it provides its 
9  licensor for review and approval prior to sale distribution.  The Court finds that like terms 
10  of a licensing agreement providing royalty rates and minimum guarantees, terms detailing 
11  the  process  through  which  Upper  Deck—as  licensee  of  certain  intellectual  property 
12  assets—submits its products for review by its licensor can constitute a trade secret.  Those 
13  terms provide a blueprint for product development strategy, which if revealed, could 
14  provide competitors an economic advantage.  In re Hydroxycut Mktg. & Sales Practices 
15  Litig., No. 09md2087 BTM (AJB), 2011 WL 864897, *2 (S.D. Cal. Mar. 11, 2011) (finding 
16  compelling  reasons  to  seal  documents  containing  information  revealing  business  and 
17  marketing strategy and product development); see also In re ConAgra Foods, Inc., No. 
18  CV1105379MMMAGRX, 2014 WL 12577132, at *5 (C.D. Cal. July 11, 2014) (finding 
19  compelling reasons to seal given “the inclusion of trade secrets such as a company's internal 
20  strategies, marketing research, sales data, and product development plans”).  Accordingly, 
21  the Court GRANTS sealing the number of samples for review and approval.   
22                      c.   Signature-Related Terms                          
23       Upper  Deck  further  moves  to  redact  the  number  of  signatures  and  signature 
24  alternatives that its licensor agreed for Michael Jordan to contribute for the development 
25  of Upper Deck’s products and services.  Here, the Court also finds that terms related to the 
26  provision of signatures are part of the product development process.  In re Hydroxycut 
27  Mktg. & Sales Practices Litig., 2011 WL 864897, *2 (finding compelling reasons to seal 
28                                                                            
1  documents containing information revealing business and marketing strategy and product 
2  development).  Accordingly, the Court GRANTS sealing signature-related terms. 
3                      d.   Personal Services Rendered by Michael Jordan     
4       Upper Deck further moves to redact personal services (e.g., autograph sessions) that 
5  its licensor agreed for Michael Jordan to contribute for the development of Upper Deck’s 
6  products and services.  Here, the Court also finds that terms related to the provision of 
7  personal services are part of the business and product development processes.  In re 
8  Hydroxycut Mktg. & Sales Practices Litig., 2011 WL 864897, *2 (finding compelling 
9  reasons  to  seal  documents  containing  information  revealing  business  and  marketing 
10  strategy and product development).  Accordingly, the Court GRANTS sealing personal 
11  service-related terms.                                                    
12                      e.   Third-Party Information (e.g., Names)            
13       The identities of third parties are generally not sealable as trade secrets unless the 
14  movant “provide[s] a particularized showing that specific harm will result if the [identities 
15  are] made publicly available.”  Apple Inc. v. Samsung Elecs. Co., No. 11-CV-01846 LHK 
16  PSG, 2012 WL 4120541, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 18, 2012); see also Fitzhenry-Russell v. 
17  Dr. Pepper Snapple Grp., Inc., No. 17-CV-00564 NC, 2018 WL 10472795, at *2 (N.D. 
18  Cal. Apr. 23, 2018) (“The identity of Dr. Pepper's third-party vender, Givaudan is not 
19  sealable as a trade secret under the compelling reasons standard”).  Here, Upper Deck has 
20  not provided any justification for how revealing the identities of third parties in the 
21  contracts would result in particularized harm to its market position.  Further, Upper Deck 
22  has failed to allege how third-party information involves any other privacy interests that 
23  “outweigh the traditional right of public access” in Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1178.  See also 
24  Bunsow De Mory LLP v. N. Forty Consulting LLC, No. 20-CV-04997-JSC, 2021 WL 
25  4521143, at *7 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 22, 2021) (rejecting motion to seal because “the names of 
26  third-parties in this action constitute neither trade secrets nor confidential information”).  
27  Though the identities of third parties in licensing agreements may be sealable in some 
28  circumstance, such as when the “existence of the agreement[s]. . .  [are] not otherwise 
1  publicly known,” Upper Deck has failed to allege any such circumstances here.  See 
2  Huawei Techs., Co, Ltd v. Samsung Elecs. Co, Ltd., 340 F. Supp. 3d 934, 1004 (N.D. Cal. 
3  2018).  Thus, the Court DENIES WITHOUT PREJUDICE Upper Deck’s requested   
4  redactions of third-party information.                                    
5                      f.   Sublicenses, Dates, Term Lengths of Agreements   
6       Boilerplate contract terms are generally not sealable.  Virun, Inc. v. Cymbiotika, 
7  LLC, No. 822CV00325SSSDFMX, 2022 WL 17401698, at *2 (C.D. Cal. Aug. 19, 2022).  
8  “Form contracts . . . that do not contain any confidential information may nevertheless be 
9  sealed if” their dissemination would create a competitive disadvantage.  Id.  The excerpts 
10  Upper Deck seeks to seal regarding sublicensing, agreement dates, and agreement term 
11  lengths  are  common  provisions  in  licensing  agreements.    Cf  Novartis  Vaccines  & 
12  Diagnostics, Inc. v. Genentech, Inc., No. 5:21-CV-04874-EJD, 2022 WL 689005, at *2 
13  (N.D. Cal. Feb. 14, 2022) (“parties provide no support for why a general description of the 
14  nature  of  the  Licensing  Agreement—particularly  a  general  description  that  reveals 
15  provisions and terms common to virtually all patent licensing agreements—should be 
16  sealed.”)  While it may be true that competitors could gain a commercial advantage upon 
17  discovering the term length of the agreements at issue in this litigation, Upper Deck has 
18  not made a particularized showing of why that may be beyond merely noting that the 
19  aforementioned terms constitute trade secrets.  See In re Sotera Wireless, Inc., 591 B.R. 
20  453, 462 (S.D. Cal. 2018), aff'd, 794 F. App'x 625 (9th Cir. 2020) (“[T]he mere statement 
21  that something is a trade secret falls far short of what the Court needs to find that [movant] 
22  has met its burden of proof. . .”).  Additionally, Upper Deck does not provide additional 
23  reasoning for why such terms should be sealed—meaning Upper Deck has failed to 
24  overcome the presumption of public access.  Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1178.  Thus, the Court 
25  DENIES WITHOUT PREJUDICE Upper Deck’s requests to redact provisions regarding 
26  sublicensing, agreement dates, and agreement term lengths.                
27                      g.   Damages-Related  Licensing  Terms  (e.g.,  Related  to 
28                      Violation)                                            
1       Upper Deck has failed to provide particularized justification for why licensing 
2  provisions relating to damages constitute either trade secrets or confidential information.  
3  See In re Sotera Wireless, Inc., 591 B.R. at 462 (“[T]he mere statement that something is 
4  a trade secret falls far short of what the Court needs to find that [movant] has met its burden 
5  of proof. . .”); cf GoDaddy.com LLC v. RPost Commc'ns Ltd., No. CV-14-00126-PHX-
6  JAT, 2016 WL 1158851, at *5 (D. Ariz. Mar. 24, 2016) (“Whether Mr. Smith properly 
7  apportioned damages is an issue that GoDaddy strongly disputes. . . and thus, the public 
8  has a high interest in this information to understand the judicial process. In the absence of 
9  compelling reasons as to why this information merits sealing, the Court will not authorize 
10  Exhibit 4 to be sealed.”).                                                
11       Thus, the Court finds Upper Deck has failed to meet its burden of proof to overcome 
12  the  “traditional  right  of  public  access,”  Kamakana,  447  F.3d  at  1178,  and  DENIES 
13  WITHOUT PREJUDICE Upper Deck’s request to seal damages provisions of licensing 
14  agreements.                                                               
15                 iii.  Lease Agreement Terms                                
16       Upper Deck moves to seal portions of ECF Nos. 75, 78, Ex. 10 regarding commercial 
17  lease agreements, including the text detailing the amount of security deposit, length of term 
18  of the agreement, and the amount of rent.  Courts within the Ninth Circuit have held that, 
19  without further explaining why terms of a lease should be subject to sealing, movants 
20  cannot “outweigh the traditional right of public access” by merely stating that such terms 
21  are  confidential.    MTO  Summerlin  LLC  v.  Shops  at  Summerlin  N.,  LP,  No. 
22  218CV00737GMNPAL, 2019 WL 1261105, at *4 (D. Nev. Mar. 19, 2019) (applying 
23  Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1178).  Similarly, here, Upper Deck does not explain how lease 
24  terms in the record constitute either trade secrets or otherwise confidential information that 
25  should be sealed beyond merely stating they should be sealed due to “privacy” concerns.  
26  Thus, the Court DENIES WITHOUT PREJUDICE Upper Deck’s proposed redactions 
27  to seal lease terms.                                                      
28                 iv.  Jordan Signature                                      
1       Upper Deck also moves to redact Jordan’s signature from ECF Nos. 75, 78, Ex. 7.  
2  However,  Upper  Deck  has  failed  to  allege  that  Jordan’s  signature  is  “not  readily 
3  ascertainable from a public source” such that it is a trade secret, or that such data should 
4  be protected on any other ground of confidentiality.  See Yeiser Rsch. & Dev. LLC , 281 F. 
5  Supp. 3d at 1046.  In absence of any particularized showing, the Court finds that Upper 
6  Deck has not met its burden of proof to overcome the presumption of public access. 
7  Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1179.                                               
8                 v.   Exhibit 105                                           
9       “An unsupported assertion of ‘unfair advantage’ to competitors without explaining 
10  ‘how  a  competitor  would  use  th[e]  information  to  obtain  an  unfair  advantage’  is

13  email chain discussion would be “advantageous for competitors and unscrupulous actors

6  II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                       
7       “[T]he courts of this country recognize a general right to inspect and copy public 
8  records and documents, including judicial records and documents.”  Nixon v. Warner 
9  Commc’ns, Inc.,
435 U.S. 589, 597
 (1978).  “Unless a particular court record is one 
10  ‘traditionally kept secret,’ a ‘strong presumption in favor of access’ is the starting point.” 
11  Kamakana v. City & Cnty. of Honolulu,
447 F.3d 1172
, 1178 (9th Cir. 2006) (citing Foltz 
12  v. State Farm Mut. Auto Ins. Co.,
331 F.3d 1122, 1135
 (9th Cir. 2003)).  “The presumption 
13  of  access  is  ‘based  on  the  need  for  federal  courts,  although  independent—indeed, 
14  particularly because they are independent—to have a measure of accountability and for the 
15  public to have confidence in the administration of justice.’”  Ctr. for Auto Safety v. Chrysler 
16  Grp., LLC,
809 F.3d 1092, 1096
 (9th Cir. 2016) (quoting United States v. Amodeo,
71 F.3d 17 1044, 1048
 (2d Cir. 1995)).                                               
18       A party seeking to seal a judicial record bears the burden of overcoming the strong 
19  presumption of access.  Foltz,
331 F.3d at 1135
. The showing required to meet this burden 
20  depends upon whether the documents to be sealed relate to a motion that is “more than 
21  tangentially related to the merits of the case.”  Ctr. for Auto Safety,
809 F.3d at 1101
.  When 
22  the underlying motion is more than tangentially related to the merits, the “compelling 
23  reasons” standard applies.
Id.
 at 1096–98.  When the underlying motion does not surpass 
24  the tangential relevance threshold, the “good cause” standard applies.
Id.
 
25       “In general, ‘compelling reasons’ sufficient to outweigh the public’s interest in 
26  disclosure and justify sealing court records exist when such ‘court files might have become 
27  a vehicle for improper purposes,’ such as the use of records to gratify private spite, promote 
28  public scandal, circulate libelous statements, or release trade secrets.”  Kamakana, 447 
1  F.3d at 1179 (quoting Nixon,
435 U.S. at 598
).  As to this last category, courts have been 
2  willing to seal court filings containing confidential business material, “such as marketing 
3  strategies, product development plans, licensing agreements, and profit, cost, and margin 
4  data,” where the parties have been able to point to concrete factual information to justify 
5  sealing.  See, e.g., Cohen v. Trump, No. 13-cv-2519-GPC-WVG,
2016 WL 3036302
, at *5 
6  (S.D. Cal. May 27, 2016).  However, “[t]he mere fact that the production of records may 
7  lead to a litigant’s embarrassment, incrimination, or exposure to further litigation will not, 
8  without  more,  compel  the  court  to  seal  its  records.”    Kamakana,  447  F.3d  at  1179. 
9  Similarly, it is not enough to “mention[] a general category of privilege, without any further 
10  elaboration or any specific linkage with the documents.”  Id. at 1184.  A blanket protective 
11  order is not itself sufficient to show “good cause,” let alone compelling reasons, for sealing 
12  particular documents.  See Foltz,
331 F.3d at 1133
; San Jose Mercury News, Inc. v. U.S. 
13  Dist. Ct., N. Dist.,
187 F.3d 1096
, 1103 (9th Cir. 1999).  The decision to seal documents is 
14  “one best left to the sound discretion of the trial court” upon consideration of the “relevant 
15  facts and circumstances of the particular case.”  Nixon,
435 U.S. at 599
. 
16       In addition, parties moving to seal documents must comply with the procedures set 
17  forth in this Court’s Standing Order for filing documents under seal.  See Standing Order 
18  of the Hon. Cynthia Bashant for Civil Cases § 5.  These procedures limit sealing to “only 
19  those documents, or portions thereof, necessary to protect such sensitive information.”  Id. 
20  Thus,  although  sometimes  it  may  be  appropriate  to  seal  a  document  in  its  entirety, 
21  whenever possible, a party must redact.  See Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1183 (noting a 
22  preference for redactions so long as they “have the virtue of being limited and clear”); 
23  Murphy v. Kavo Am. Corp., No. 11-cv-00410-YGR,
2012 WL 1497489
, at *2–3 (N.D. Cal. 
24  Apr. 27, 2012) (denying motion to seal exhibits but directing parties to redact confidential 
25  information).

18            2.   “Compelling Reasons” Legal Standard                        
19       Preventing the release of trade secrets generally constitutes a compelling reason to 
20  seal such documents.  Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1179; see also Nixon,
435 U.S. at 598
 
21  (observing that the “common-law right of inspection has bowed before the power of a court 
22  to insure that its records” are not used as “sources of business information that might harm 
23  a litigant's competitive standing”);  Apple Inc. v. Samsung Elecs. Co.,
727 F.3d 1214
, 1226–
24  28  (Fed.Cir.2013)  (holding  that  under  Ninth  Circuit  law,  detailed  product-specific 
25  information and internal reports are appropriate to seal under the “compelling reasons” 
26  standard where that information could be used to the company's competitive disadvantage). 
27       A  “trade  secret  may  consist  of  any  formula,  pattern,  device  or  compilation  of 
28  information  which  is  used  in  [the  party]'s  business,  and  which  gives  [the  party]  an 
1  opportunity to obtain an advantage over competitors who do not know or use it.”  In re 
2  Elec. Arts, Inc.,
298 F. App'x 568
, 569–70 (9th Cir. 2008) (citing Restatement of Torts § 
3  757, cmt. B); see also Clark v. Bunker,
453 F.2d 1006, 1009
 (9th Cir.1972) (adopting the 
4  Restatement  definition  and  finding  that  “a  detailed  plan  for  the  creation,  promotion, 
5  financing, and sale of contracts” constitutes a trade secret); Whyte v. Schlage Lock Co., 101
6 Cal.App.4th 1443, 1455-56
,
125 Cal.Rptr.2d 277
 (2002).                    
7       Even if proposed material for sealing does not constitute a trade secret, it may still 
8  be sealable as confidential business information.  See In re Elec. Arts, Inc.,
298 F. App'x at 9
  569  (finding  sealable  “business  information  that  might  harm  a  litigant's  competitive 
10  standing”); see also Ctr. for Auto Safety,
809 F.3d at 1097
 (citing Nixon, 435 U.S. at 598–
11  599) (“sources of business information that might harm a litigant's competitive standing” 
12  are subject to sealing); see also In re Qualcomm Litig., No. 3:17-cv-0108-GPC-MDD, 2017
13 WL 5176922
, at *2 (S.D. Cal. Nov. 8, 2017) (sealing is warranted to prevent competitors 
14  from “gaining insight into the parties' business model and strategy”); see also Garrity 
15  Power Servs. LLC v. Samsung Elecs. Co., No. 21-MC-80159-JSC,
2021 WL 3473937
, at 
16  *1 (N.D. Cal. July 29, 2021) (“confidential business information in the form of ‘license 
17  agreements, financial terms, details of confidential licensing negotiations, and business 
18  strategies’ is sealable”).                                                
19       However, not all business information is so confidential or sensitive that it must be 
20  sealed.  See, e.g., Open Text S.A. v. Box, Inc., No. 13-04910,
2014 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 21
  177484,
2014 WL 7368594
, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Dec. 26, 2014) (declining to seal, for example, 
22  information about a litigant's "product design and source code and highly confidential and 
23  competitively sensitive business information including usage data," in the absence of 
24  demonstrating “specific compelling reasons”); GoDaddy.com LLC v. RPost Commc'ns 
25  Ltd., No. 14-00126,
2014 WL 2117349
, at *1 (D. Ariz. May 21, 2014) ("[A] party's 
26  allegations that material is 'confidential' or 'business information' are insufficient to justify 
27  sealing court records containing such material unless the party proves the existence of 
28                                                                            
1  compelling reasons such as those set forth in Kamakana.... "[O]nly in extremely limited 
2  circumstances will confidential information actually merit the sealing of court records.").  
3       In the Ninth Circuit, trade secrets, specific pricing terms, royalty rates, and similar 
4  data are commonly sealed.  See, e.g., In re Elec. Arts, Inc.,
298 F. App'x 568, 569
 (9th 
5  Cir. 2008).  For information that falls outside of those categories, movants must 
6  particularly allege how their proposed redactions relate to confidential information that 
7  should be sealed.  See Perez v. Blue Mountain Farms, No. 2:13-CV-5081-RMP, 2015
8 WL 11112413
, at *4 (E.D. Wash. Sept. 28, 2015) (“Defendants' redactions and any 
9  claims of privilege or withholding of information must be explained with particularity as 
10  to why that information should be protected pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5)(A)”); see 
11  also Ketayi v. Health Enrollment Grp., No. 3:20-CV-1198-RSH-KSC,
2023 WL 12
  12007132, at *2 (S.D. Cal. June 28, 2023)  (“Compelling reasons may exist to seal some 
13  of the redacted information in this record as confidential business information, but not for 
14  the broad redactions HII proposes.”).                                     
15       Importantly, “[t]he proponent of sealing bears the burden with respect to sealing. A 
16  failure to meet that burden means that the default posture of public access prevails.”  
17  Kamakana v. City & County of Honolulu,
447 F.3d 1172
, 1182 (9th Cir. 2006). 
18            3.   “Narrowly Tailored” Legal Standard                         
19       “Only those documents, or portions thereof, necessary to protect such sensitive 
20  information” may be sealed. Standing Order § 5.A. As such, whenever possible, the 
21  moving party must redact only what is necessary.  See Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1183; 
22  Murphy,
2012 WL 1497489
, at *2–3.  Redactions must be narrowly tailored such that only 
23  information that meets the compelling reasons standard is redacted. See Kamakana, 447 
24  F.3d at 1183 (highlighting the “limited and clear” nature and specificity of the redactions); 
25  ImprimisRx, LLC v. OSRX, Inc., No. 21-cv-01305-BAS-DL,
2023 WL 7029210
, at *4 
26  (S.D. Cal. Oct. 24, 2023) (rejecting redactions that were insufficiently tailored). The 
27  moving party must provide the compelling reason justifying the proposed redactions. Foltz, 
28
331 F.3d at 1135
.

2  Inc. v. Phillips Cattle Co., Inc., No. 24-cv-01299-BAS-MSB,
2024 WL 4280960

4  agreements in order to understand the court’s rulings.
Id.

5  ambiguous references to sealed documents, without any discussion of the substance of the

7  N.A., No. 21-cv-1799-BAS-BGS,
2024 WL 171659
, at *9 (S.D. Cal. Jan. 12, 2024); 
8  ImprimisRx, LLC,
2023 WL 7029210
, at *5.  Information already available to the public 
9  also cannot meet the compelling reasons standard.  See
id. at 1184
.

15  Rsch. & Dev. LLC v. Teknor Apex Co.,
281 F. Supp. 3d 1021
, 1046 (S.D. Cal. 2017).  Here,

25                 ii.  Licensing Agreement Terms                             
26       The Ninth Circuit has held that licensing agreement terms are sealable trade secrets 
27  when such terms provide a plan for the formation and sale of contracts.  In re Elec. Arts, 
28  Inc., 298 F. App'x at 569–70 (finding license agreement to be a trade secret); France 
1  Telecom S.A. v. Marvell Semiconductor Inc., No. 12-CV-04967-WHO,
2014 WL 4965995
, 
2  at *3 (N.D. Cal. Oct. 3, 2014) (“the information at issue—terms of a license agreement—
3  constitutes trade secrets and is properly sealed”).  Those terms may constitute trade secrets 
4  because their public disclosure may hinder the trade secret holder’s market competitiveness 
5  and participation.  See e.g., In re NCAA Student-Athlete Name & Likeness Licensing Litig., 
6  No. C 09-1967 CW,
2014 WL 662545
, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Feb. 20, 2014) (“Because the public 
7  disclosure of some of these terms may undermine NCAA's ability to negotiate future 
8  licensing agreements with other broadcasters, these terms may be sealed.”).  
9       However, there are limitations on the extent to which terms of a licensing agreement 
10  can be sealed.  For example, if certain terms are “otherwise publicly known,” they may not 
11  be sealable.  Huawei Techs., Co, Ltd v. Samsung Elecs. Co, Ltd.,
340 F. Supp. 3d 934
, 1004 
12  (N.D.  Cal.  2018).    Additionally,  if  terms  of  licensing  agreements  that  appear  to  be 
13  boilerplate contractual terms, courts may require the moving party to “explain[] why 
14  [those] provisions are so unique to that agreement that disclosure would cause significant 
15  harm.”
Id.

16  secrets, they have still limited permissible redactions to only specific portions of those 
17  clauses.  In re NCAA Student-Athlete Name & Likeness Licensing Litig.,
2014 WL 662545
, 
18  at *1 (“only the specific dollar amounts. . . may be sealed”); O'Bannon v. Nat'l Collegiate 
19  Athletic Ass'n, No. C 09-3329 CW,
2014 WL 12997312
, at *1 (N.D. Cal. June 10, 2014) 
20  (same).

16       Upper Deck moves to seal portions of ECF Nos. 75, 78, Ex. 10 regarding commercial 
17  lease agreements, including the text detailing the amount of security deposit, length of term 
18  of the agreement, and the amount of rent.  Courts within the Ninth Circuit have held that, 
19  without further explaining why terms of a lease should be subject to sealing, movants 
20  cannot “outweigh the traditional right of public access” by merely stating that such terms 
21  are  confidential.    MTO  Summerlin  LLC  v.  Shops  at  Summerlin  N.,  LP,  No. 
22  218CV00737GMNPAL,
2019 WL 1261105
, at *4 (D. Nev. Mar. 19, 2019) (applying 
23  Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1178).  Similarly, here, Upper Deck does not explain how lease 
24  terms in the record constitute either trade secrets or otherwise confidential information that 
25  should be sealed beyond merely stating they should be sealed due to “privacy” concerns.  
26  Thus, the Court DENIES WITHOUT PREJUDICE Upper Deck’s proposed redactions 
27  to seal lease terms.
